content: The European Medicines Agency (EMA) is a European organization responsible for the evaluation of medicinal products. Prior to 2004, it was known as the European Agency for the Evaluation of Medicinal Products. Established in 1995, the EMA was created with funding from the European Union, the pharmaceutical industry, and indirect subsidies from member states. Its purpose is to harmonize, but not replace, the work of national medicine regulatory bodies across Europe. Unlike the centralized model of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the EMA operates as a decentralized scientific agency. The EMA aims to reduce the $350 million annual cost incurred by pharmaceutical companies seeking separate approvals from each EU member state. Additionally, it seeks to eliminate protectionist tendencies of states that may resist approving new drugs competing with domestically produced ones. The European Union is currently responsible for approximately one-third of the new drugs introduced to the global market each year. Headquartered in London, the EMA was established after over seven years of negotiations among EU governments. It replaced the Committee for Proprietary Medicinal Products (established in 1977) and the Committee for Veterinary Medicinal Products, both of which were restructured as core scientific advisory committees. The agency was initially set up under EC Regulation No. 2309/93 as the European Agency for the Evaluation of Medicinal Products and was renamed under EC Regulation No. 726/2004 as the European Medicines Agency, retaining the acronym EMA. The EMA functions as a decentralized scientific agency of the EU, focusing on the protection and promotion of human and animal health. It achieves this through the coordination of evaluation and monitoring of centrally authorized products and national referrals, the development of technical guidance, and the provision of scientific advice to sponsors. Its scope includes medicinal products for human and veterinary use, biologics, tissue-engineered products (TEPs), and herbal medicinal products. The agency is structured into four units: human medicine, veterinary medicines and inspections, communications and networking, and administration. It is overseen by a Management Board, which provides administrative oversight, approves budgets and plans, and selects the Executive Director. The board includes two members from each EU member state, two from the European Economic Community (EEC), and two from the European Parliament. For products requiring central approval, pharmaceutical companies submit marketing authorization applications to the EMA. A single evaluation is conducted by the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) or the Committee for Medicinal Products for Veterinary Use (CVMP). If the relevant committee concludes that the product's quality, safety, and efficacy are sufficiently proven, it adopts a positive opinion. This opinion is then forwarded to the European Commission, which issues a marketing authorization valid across the entire EU. The EMA also administers the granting of orphan drug status through its Committee on Orphan Medicinal Products (COMP). Additionally, the Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) assists in harmonizing procedures and provisions for herbal medicinal products across EU member states, further integrating these products into the European regulatory framework. A new committee addressing pediatric legislation in Europe was planned to be operational by the third quarter of 2007. While most existing medicines in EU member states remain authorized nationally, the majority of genuinely novel medicines are authorized through the EMA. The agency employs approximately 500 staff members and decentralizes its scientific assessments by utilizing a computer-linked network of around 3,500 experts across the EU. It draws on the resources of National Competent Authorities (NCAs) in EU member states. The CHMP and CVMP are required by regulation to reach decisions within 210 days. However, this timeline may be paused if additional clarification or supporting data is needed from the applicant.
